analysis.one_liner: Imposes uniform national limits on injury lawsuits, making losing plaintiffs pay the winners' legal fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced by Sen. Mitch McConnell with two cosponsors in June 1989, it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and its courts subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state tort law with one set of national rules for lawsuits over injuries from products, services, and accidents. It would have abolished joint and several liability so each defendant pays only its own share of fault, made a claimant's intoxication a complete defense in many cases, and required the loser of a lawsuit to pay the winner's legal fees. It would also have preempted state laws, restricted civil rights suits against local governments, and barred most organizations from suing under the main federal civil rights statute.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing injury and malpractice lawsuits, the liability insurance industry, medical providers, and local governments. Companies would face smaller and more predictable payouts because each defendant would pay only its own share of fault, an intoxicated claimant could lose outright, and the threat of paying the other side's fees would discourage marginal suits. Local governments would be shielded from punitive damages and from damages for good-faith actions under the federal civil rights statute.

how_it_helps.text: Abolishes joint and several liability: a defendant found partly at fault pays only its own share, not the whole judgment when other wrongdoers cannot pay.
Makes a claimant's intoxication a complete defense when the claimant was more than 50 percent responsible for the accident.
Requires the losing party to pay the prevailing party's costs and attorney's fees, with caps and an exception for people eligible for Legal Services assistance.

Amends the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to bar most organizations from suing, prohibit damages against local governments for good-faith acts, and prohibit punitive damages against local governments.
Preempts and supersedes inconsistent federal and state laws, replacing dozens of different state liability rules with one national standard.
Reduces damage awards by workers' compensation benefits in product liability cases and bars third parties from seeking indemnity or contribution from employers in most circumstances.

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products, malpractice, or accidents. Loser-pays fee shifting would make an ordinary person think twice before suing a well-funded company, since losing could mean paying the company's legal bills. Abolishing joint and several liability means that when one responsible party is insolvent or unidentified, the injured person absorbs the shortfall. Limits on civil rights suits would leave people with fewer remedies against local governments.
analysis.who_pays_short: People injured by products or malpractice

drawbacks.text: Requiring losers to pay winners' attorney fees would deter injured people of ordinary means from bringing legitimate claims, because losing to a well-funded defendant could cost them the defendant's legal fees.

Federal preemption would override state tort law, including stronger consumer protections some states had adopted, and the bill would apply immediately to all suits filed after enactment even for older conduct.

The complete intoxication defense could bar recovery even where the defendant was also negligent, and the changes to the civil rights statute would narrow remedies for people whose rights are violated by local governments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give businesses and insurers predictability and lower litigation costs, and some features (like promoting mediation) are uncontroversial. But the core provisions shift risk away from companies and governments and onto injured people: loser-pays fee shifting, the intoxication defense, the end of joint and several liability, and retroactive application would make it substantially harder and riskier for an ordinary person to be made whole after an injury. The bill's own stated rationale is competitiveness and insurance affordability for business, not compensation for the injured.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, then passed to its courts subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the Lawsuit Reform Act of 1989 in the Senate on June 1, 1989.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On June 13, 1989, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill had only two cosponsors, both Republican senators.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, injured people kept the existing state-law rules for suing businesses, insurers, and local governments, including joint and several liability and the American rule on legal fees. Businesses and insurers did not get the liability limits the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people kept their right to sue

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lawsuit Reform Act of 1989 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 1, 1989, passed it to a subcommittee on June 13, and never reported it back or scheduled any vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors were all Republicans and it drew no Democratic cosponsors, but it never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: Uniform national liability rules, the intoxication defense, and loser-pays fee shifting would reduce the volume and size of injury claims insurers must pay. The savings come out of compensation that injured people would otherwise recover.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and businesses facing tort suits
industries.note: Ending joint and several liability caps each defendant's payment at its own share of fault, and fee shifting would discourage suits. The bill's stated purpose is to lower liability costs for American companies.

The bill would bar punitive damages and damages for good-faith acts against local governments under the federal civil rights statute, and would block most organizations from suing on behalf of others. Residents would have fewer ways to hold governments financially accountable.

Contingency-fee practice depends on injured people being able to sue and recover; loser-pays rules and preempting state law would sharply cut the volume and value of cases. The bar's income comes from recovering compensation for ordinary clients.

industries.industry: Health care providers and malpractice insurers
industries.note: Proportional liability and fee shifting would lower malpractice exposure and insurance costs, but there is no evidence in the bill's findings that savings would reach patients as lower prices. The cost falls on injured patients who recover less.
